prime.problem: Thousands of customers each want their own fine-tune of the same base model, but each gets too little traffic to fill a GPU. Merging each fine-tune into its own model copy splits every batch by customer and multiplies memory; serving them one at a time serialises the traffic.
prime.fits: A serving feature that leans on the scheduler (iteration-level batching) and course 4's paging. It asks how one batch can serve many different adapters without losing the shared weight read that makes batching pay.
expect: LoRA as x·A·B beside the shared x·W
unified paging of adapters and KV (S-LoRA)
adapter bytes as extra per-step reads
prime.goal: Compute an adapter's size and per-step cost on the running example, and explain why unmerged adapters plus a gather kernel keep batching intact.

attend: Why does merging W′ = W + AB, perfect for one adapter, break continuous batching across many?
What does SGMV do with a batch whose rows use three different adapters, and how many launches does it take?
Why can adapters and KV cache share one paged pool in S-LoRA?
When 64 requests use 64 different adapters, what extra bytes does each step read, and why does grouping by adapter help?
Why is the tensor-parallel communication for LoRA so small compared with the base model's?

must: Continuous batching pays because every request multiplies the same W → one weight read serves the whole batch → merged adapters give each request its own W′ → batches split by adapter (baselines ran at batch 1–3) → keep W shared and add each request's small x·A·B instead

Sort the batch into segments by adapter → one GEMM for x·W → one SGMV shrink and one expand launch cover every adapter (adapter index on blockIdx.y) → mixed-adapter batches run at about base speed (1,044 vs 1,140 tok/s on 7B)

Each distinct adapter adds its own A and B reads per step → 27.26 MB at r = 16 → 64 distinct adapters add 1.74 GB, +10.9% of the base read → requests that share an adapter share its read → adapter clustering trades fairness for fewer bytes

An adapter of rank R and a KV cache of S tokens are both rows of width H → one pre-allocated pool holds both in pages → loading adapters of mixed ranks doesn't fragment memory → thousands of adapters live in host RAM and only active ones are paged in (2,000 at 7.61 req/s)
elevated: Computing (x·A)·B costs 2·r·(d_in + d_out) FLOPs per token, never the d_in·d_out of forming AB → 0.17% of the base FLOPs at r = 16
reference: vLLM flags and defaults (--enable-lora, max_loras = 1, max_lora_rank = 16, max_cpu_loras)

compress.prompt: Draw the Fig 3-style batch from memory: four rows, three adapters, one shared GEMM and the two SGMV launches. Beside it, write the adapter-size formula for Llama-3.1-8B on q/k/v/o and one line on what unified paging adds.
checklist: params = r × 26,624 × 32 layers; r = 16 → 13.6M params, 27.26 MB
one shrink and one expand launch for all adapters in the batch
distinct adapters cost reads; shared ones don't
adapters and KV in one paged pool; the catalog in host RAM, with prefetch

retrieve.q: Explain why keeping adapters unmerged is what lets requests for different fine-tunes share a batch.
answer: unmerged, every request multiplies the same base W, so one weight read serves all
the adapter part is a small extra computation per request
merged, each adapter is a different full weight matrix, so requests can't share a GEMM

retrieve.q: Walk through q_proj for a 4-request batch using adapters A, B, A, C: sorting, the base GEMM, shrink, expand, and the bytes read.
answer: sort rows so both A requests are adjacent: segments A, B, C
one GEMM with W (33.6 MB read once)
SGMV shrink: each segment × its own A_i (4096 → 16), one launch
SGMV expand: × B_i (16 → 4096), added to the base output, one launch
adapter reads: three adapters at 0.26 MB each (+2.3%)

retrieve.q: A product has one popular fine-tune with steady heavy traffic plus 500 rarely used ones. How would you serve each group, and why not the same way?
answer: the popular one: merge it and serve as a plain model at zero overhead
the long tail: shared base with unmerged adapters, S-LoRA-style paging from host RAM
multi-LoRA pays when each adapter alone can't fill a GPU; costs are extra kernels, distinct-adapter reads and cold loads

compare.q: PagedAttention pages the KV cache; S-LoRA pages adapters in the same pool. What property of the two data types makes one pool possible, and what goes wrong if adapters sit in a separate contiguous region?
answer: both are rows of width H: S rows for S tokens of KV, R rows for a rank-R adapter
one pool with fixed-size pages serves both, with no fragmentation between them
a separate region would fragment as adapters of different ranks come and go, and memory can't flow between KV and adapters as load shifts

compare.q: Per-request adapters and per-request grammar masks both add work that grows with the batch. Where does each cost land (GPU bytes or CPU time), and which trick hides each?
answer: adapters: extra GPU reads and small kernels per distinct adapter; grouping by adapter and a shared pool reduce them
masks: CPU time per request per step; precomputation plus overlap with the forward pass hide them
both grow with B, so both matter most at large batch

predict.q: Raise the rank from 16 to 32 with 64 distinct adapters in every step. Does the per-step overhead double, and does the adapter share of FLOPs matter? Commit first.
predict.answer: Yes, the bytes double: each adapter is 54.5 MB, 64 of them 3.49 GB, about 1.04 ms or +21.7% on the 4.79 ms weight read (our recomputation), and r = 64 gives +43%. The FLOPs stay tiny (0.34% at r = 32), so at decode it's the bytes of distinct adapters that cost you, not their math.

apply.task: Run labs/lora-cost.py, then use its formula by hand for r = 32 on q/k/v/o: adapter size, how many fit in the 63.9 GB of free HBM at r = 16, the extra read for 64 distinct r = 32 adapters per step, and the S-LoRA tensor-parallel communication ratio 5r ÷ 2h at r = 64 with h = 4,096.
apply.done: An adapter size, a fit count, a per-step overhead in ms and %, and a TP ratio, before checking.
apply.hint: Check after trying (our recomputation): r = 32 → 54.53 MB; r = 16 fits ≈ 2,343 adapters in 63.9 GB (leaving no KV); 64 distinct r = 32 adapters → 3.49 GB → 1.04 ms, +21.7%; TP ratio 320 ÷ 8,192 ≈ 3.9% more traffic.
